Tracking Shai-Hulud: Inside the ChainDrop NPM Worm
zscaler.com · 11 Aug 2026 21:21 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
TAGSchaindropetherhidinggithubhadeskeyvmegalodonmiasmamini-shai-huludnpmphantom-gyppull-request-targetpwn-requestrussiashai-huludteampcp
96
In plain words

The article describes ChainDrop, a malicious program that got into the npm software ecosystem after an attacker took over a maintainer’s GitHub account for the keyv ecosystem and used the project’s normal release process to publish tainted versions of several packages. Developers and companies that installed those packages could have had account tokens, cloud keys, source code access, and other secrets stolen, and the malware then used that access to infect more than 400 other packages. It matters because the poisoned packages looked like legitimate releases, showing that even trusted build records and signed releases can fail when an attacker controls the account or project that creates them.

Summary
ChainDrop is a self-propagating npm worm that abused a compromised maintainer account and trusted GitHub Actions release pipelines to publish malicious packages with valid provenance, then stole developer tokens to spread to more than 400 packages. Its use of Ethereum-based C2, IDE/AI-tool persistence hooks, and destructive token-revocation behavior shows that signed builds and SLSA attestations alone cannot guarantee package safety.

On August 4, 2026, a self-propagating worm called ChainDrop entered the npm ecosystem through a compromised maintainer account in the keyv ecosystem. The attacker injected malicious code into the legitimate source repositories and triggered GitHub Actions release workflows to publish poisoned versions of packages including keyv, cacheable, flat-cache, and file-entry-cache. Aikido Security researchers found that the worm propagated to more than 400 packages.

ChainDrop is significant because some malicious packages, most notably keyv@6.0.0, carried authentic SLSA provenance attestations after being built and published by the legitimate repository workflow. The article emphasizes that a signed origin does not guarantee safe content when the attacker controls the source repository or build process. The worm spread by stealing npm tokens and republishing infected versions of every package those tokens could reach, reaching a peak of roughly one infected package per second.

Technically, ChainDrop used a preinstall hook to run setup.mjs, download the Bun runtime, and execute the obfuscated Math_Symbol.js payload. The payload harvested credentials including npm tokens, GitHub credentials, cloud keys, Kubernetes credentials, HashiCorp Vault tokens, SSH keys, and AI tooling credentials, then exfiltrated stolen data through GitHub dead-drop repositories or fallback Ethereum-based command-and-control. The worm also planted persistence hooks in Claude Code and Visual Studio Code configuration files and included a token-revocation trap that could wipe a victim’s home directory.

  • Valid SLSA or Sigstore provenance did not distinguish the malicious releases from clean ones because the attacker controlled the legitimate source repository and release workflow.
  • Domain blocklists and DNS sinkholes were weakened because ChainDrop retrieved fallback command-and-control domains from an Ethereum smart contract that could be updated with a blockchain transaction.
  • Removing the malicious package or using npm install with --ignore-scripts was insufficient because ChainDrop also planted hooks in IDE and AI-agent configuration files that could re-execute the payload when a project was opened.
  • Revoking exposed tokens could trigger a destructive response from the worm, so incident response had to account for the article’s described token-monitoring process and possible home-directory wipe.
  • AI-based package scanning pipelines could be manipulated because earlier related variants embedded prompt-injection instructions, and the article recommends treating scanner refusals or missing verdicts as escalation signals rather than clean results.
Key Points
  • 01On August 4, 2026, ChainDrop entered the npm ecosystem through a compromised maintainer account in the keyv ecosystem and triggered legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows to publish poisoned package versions.
  • 02Some infected packages, most notably keyv@6.0.0, were published to npm with authentic SLSA provenance attestations because the build originated from the legitimate repository and workflow.
  • 03ChainDrop stole npm tokens and other developer credentials, then used valid publishing rights to republish infected versions of packages, spreading to more than 400 packages in under four hours.
  • 04The worm used an Ethereum smart contract to retrieve active command-and-control domains, allowing the attacker to rotate domains without changing the deployed malware.
  • 05ChainDrop planted persistence hooks in Claude Code and Visual Studio Code configuration files and included a token-revocation trap that could trigger deletion of the victim’s home directory.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a must-read because it reports a specific, high-impact npm supply-chain worm that spread to more than 400 packages, abused trusted GitHub Actions release pipelines, and carried valid SLSA provenance. The article also details actionable technical risks including token theft, Ethereum-based command-and-control, IDE/AI-tool persistence, and destructive behavior after token revocation.

Shattering the Dream – When a Job Offer Becomes a Zero-Day Attack
research.checkpoint.com · 11 Aug 2026 17:30 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5

In plain words

Check Point Research describes a Lazarus campaign called Operation Dream Job that used fake job offers to target defense, aerospace, and aviation organizations, especially in Europe and India. Victims were tricked into opening altered PDF tools and documents that secretly installed programs giving the attackers remote access, and the attackers also used a newly discovered Windows flaw that Microsoft later patched. This matters because the campaign focused on military-related companies working on areas like surveillance sensors, drones, and robotics, and in at least one case a compromised European organization was used to send more convincing fake messages to other targets.

Summary
Check Point says Lazarus’ Operation Dream Job is targeting defense, aerospace, and aviation organizations with fake job lures, trojanized PDF viewers, and new malware including Troy and RelayShell. The campaign also used a Windows AFD.sys zero-day, CVE-2026-68820, to deploy the FudModule rootkit for SYSTEM privileges and EDR evasion.

Check Point Research is tracking a long-running Lazarus-affiliated campaign called Operation Dream Job that targets organizations worldwide, with a particular focus on the defense sector. The latest wave focuses on the defense sector in Europe and India, especially companies in aerospace and aviation. The campaign uses fake job opportunities to convince victims to download malicious files.

The article describes two active infection chains: one using DLL sideloading with a legitimate PDF viewer and malicious DLL, and another using SecurityPDF, a trojanized PDF viewer that executes encrypted payloads from crafted PDF documents. The attackers deployed malware including MISTPEN, ForestTiger, the newly identified Troy backdoor, FudModule, and RelayShell. They also used impersonation websites and search engine optimization to distribute the trojanized viewer.

During the intrusion, the threat actor exploited CVE-2026-68820, a zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft’s AFD.sys driver, to deploy a new version of the FudModule kernel-mode rootkit with SYSTEM privileges and reduce EDR visibility. Check Point Research disclosed the issue to Microsoft, which released a patch on August 11, 2026. The attackers also compromised Roundcube, WordPress, and PrestaShop servers, using RelayShell webshells to turn them into command-and-control relay nodes.

  • The attackers separated the malicious PDF document from the trojanized PDF viewer and used impersonation websites with search engine optimization, which the article says likely reduced the likelihood of detection compared with a single phishing attachment.
  • The new FudModule version no longer includes a dedicated Microsoft Defender-disabling stage, but it can still blind Microsoft Defender through a generic security-product suppression engine used against multiple vendors.
  • The article reports that FudModule v3.1 specifically checks for newer Windows 11 builds 26100 and 26200, making the campaign relevant to fully patched and current Windows 11 environments before Microsoft’s August 11, 2026 fix.
  • RelayShell was designed mainly as a relay between infected endpoints and operators rather than as a traditional direct command-execution webshell, allowing compromised web servers to blend into the attacker’s command-and-control infrastructure.
  • At least one compromised organization in France was reused to send spear-phishing messages to additional targets, showing that trusted victim infrastructure became part of the campaign’s delivery mechanism.
Key Points
  • 01Check Point Research is tracking a Lazarus-affiliated Operation Dream Job campaign that targets organizations worldwide, with a particular focus on the defense sector in Europe and India.
  • 02The campaign uses fake job opportunities to deliver malicious files, including DLL sideloading packages and a trojanized PDF viewer called SecurityPDF that executes payloads from specially crafted PDF documents.
  • 03During the intrusion, the threat actor exploited CVE-2026-68820, a zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft’s AFD.sys driver, to deploy a new version of the FudModule kernel-mode rootkit with SYSTEM privileges.
  • 04The attackers used compromised Roundcube, WordPress, and PrestaShop servers as command-and-control infrastructure, including RelayShell PHP webshells deployed on vulnerable Roundcube servers.
  • 05The campaign deployed multiple malware components, including MISTPEN, ForestTiger, the newly identified Troy backdoor, FudModule, and RelayShell.

    Microsoft August 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 400 flaws, 3 zero-days
    bleepingcomputer.com · 11 Aug 2026 18:08 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
    TAGSafd.syscheck-pointcve-2026-62832cve-2026-68820cve-2026-72971fudmodulelazaruslink-followingmicrosoftnorth-koreapatch-tuesdayrace-conditionunionfs.sysuse-after-freewindows-user-profile-service
    In plain words

    Microsoft released its August 2026 security updates to fix 400 problems across its software, including Windows, Office, Azure, Exchange, Teams, and other products. Three of the problems were already known before the fixes were available, and one Windows flaw had been used by the North Korean group Lazarus to gain the highest level of control on affected computers and install hidden malicious software. This matters because people and organizations using affected Microsoft products could be exposed to break-ins, stolen information, or attackers taking over systems if the updates are not applied.

    Summary
    Microsoft’s August 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 400 vulnerabilities, including 42 critical flaws and three zero-days. The most urgent is CVE-2026-68820, an actively exploited Windows AFD.sys privilege-escalation bug used by North Korea’s Lazarus group to deploy the FudModule rootkit.

    Microsoft’s August 2026 Patch Tuesday includes security updates for 400 flaws, including one actively exploited zero-day and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities. The release addresses 42 “Critical” vulnerabilities, made up of 37 remote code execution flaws and 5 elevation of privilege flaws. Microsoft said the total only counts fixes released on Patch Tuesday and excludes some flaws in products such as Mariner, Teams, Azure, Entra, Office, and Power Apps that were fixed earlier in the month.

    The actively exploited zero-day is CVE-2026-68820, a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock elevation of privilege vulnerability that can grant SYSTEM privileges. Microsoft described it as a use-after-free issue that a locally authenticated attacker could exploit by running a specially crafted application to trigger a race condition, with no user interaction required. Check Point said North Korean threat actors known as Lazarus exploited the flaw to deploy a new version of FudModule, Lazarus’ kernel-mode rootkit.

    Microsoft also fixed two publicly disclosed zero-days: CVE-2026-62832 in the Windows User Profile Service and CVE-2026-72971 in the Windows Container Isolation FS Filter Driver, unionfs.sys. The Windows User Profile Service issue involves improper link resolution before file access and can allow an authenticated attacker with credentials for another local account to access or modify another user’s data and gain administrator privileges. The article also notes that other vendors, including Adobe, Cisco, Metabase, N-able, SAP, TP-Link, and VMware, released security updates or advisories in August 2026.

    • Microsoft says the 400-flaw total excludes vulnerabilities in several products that were fixed earlier in the month, so organizations may need to review more than just the Patch Tuesday release to account for all recent Microsoft fixes.
    • Microsoft linked the high volume of recent Patch Tuesday fixes to its use of an AI-powered vulnerability discovery system, indicating that larger-than-usual monthly update batches may continue.
    • CVE-2026-68820 does not require user interaction, but it does require local authentication, making it especially relevant after an attacker has already gained some access to a Windows system.
    • The publicly disclosed Windows User Profile Service flaw matches the previously reported “LegacyHive” issue, which was described as allowing non-admin users to trigger administrator-level command execution when an admin logs into a compromised device.
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft’s August 2026 Patch Tuesday includes security updates for 400 flaws, including one actively exploited zero-day and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.
    • 02The updates address 42 critical vulnerabilities, consisting of 37 remote code execution flaws and 5 elevation of privilege flaws.
    • 03The actively exploited zero-day, CVE-2026-68820, is a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock vulnerability that can allow a locally authenticated attacker to gain SYSTEM privileges.
    • 04Check Point reported that North Korean threat actors known as Lazarus exploited CVE-2026-68820 to deploy a new version of the FudModule kernel-mode rootkit.
    • 05Microsoft also fixed two publicly disclosed zero-days: CVE-2026-62832 in Windows User Profile Service and CVE-2026-72971 in Windows Container Isolation FS Filter Driver unionfs.sys.

    In plain words

    Microsoft released its monthly security updates fixing 398 problems, including one in Windows that is already being used in attacks and can let someone who has already gotten onto a computer gain full control of it. The article says this matters for people and organizations using Windows systems, especially servers running Windows DNS Server, Windows Deployment Services, Microsoft QUIC, HPC Pack, or on-premises SharePoint. Some of the fixed problems could let an outsider break into certain exposed servers without needing a password or anyone to click anything, so installing the right updates quickly can reduce the chance of serious compromise.

    Summary
    Microsoft’s latest Patch Tuesday fixes 398 flaws, led by an actively exploited Windows afd.sys kernel driver zero-day that can let attackers with local code execution escalate to SYSTEM. Admins should prioritize that patch, then address exposed unauthenticated RCE flaws in DNS Server, WDS, QUIC, HPC Pack, and ensure SharePoint has both July and August fixes.

    Microsoft released its monthly security updates, fixing 398 new CVEs according to the Zero Day Initiative, including 62 rated Critical. The top priority is CVE-2026-68820, a Windows afd.sys kernel driver flaw that Microsoft says is under active exploitation. The flaw can let an attacker who already has code running on a machine escalate privileges to SYSTEM.

    Check Point Research said CVE-2026-68820 is a use-after-free in the Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock and that Lazarus used it in the Operation Dream Job campaign. Microsoft has not publicly attributed the exploitation. The release also includes four unauthenticated remote code execution flaws with CVSS scores of 9.8 affecting Windows DNS Server, Windows Deployment Services, Microsoft QUIC, and HPC Pack.

    The article emphasizes that patch priority should account for exploit status, service exposure, and whether affected services are present in an environment. It also notes that the August release closes CVE-2026-63520, the remote code execution half of a SharePoint chain whose authentication bypass, CVE-2026-55040, was fixed in July. On-premises SharePoint farms should have both the July authentication-bypass fix and the August RCE fix installed.

    • Microsoft’s patch priority is not determined by CVSS score alone, since the actively exploited CVE-2026-68820 is prioritized ahead of four 9.8-rated server flaws because attackers are already using it.
    • Service inventory and internet reachability are critical for prioritization, because the practical risk from the DNS Server, WDS, QUIC, and HPC Pack flaws depends on whether those services are present and exposed in a given environment.
    • The Zero Day Initiative’s description of the Windows DNS Server flaw as “wormable” reflects a technical condition, but the article explicitly notes that this does not mean a worm currently exists.
    • For on-premises SharePoint, the July patch for CVE-2026-55040 already broke Rapid7’s demonstrated unauthenticated RCE chain, while the August patch closes the separate RCE component.
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft released monthly security updates addressing 398 new CVEs, including 62 rated Critical according to the Zero Day Initiative.
    • 02CVE-2026-68820 is an actively exploited Windows afd.sys kernel driver flaw that can allow an attacker with code already running on a machine to escalate privileges to SYSTEM.
    • 03Check Point Research said Lazarus used CVE-2026-68820 in its Operation Dream Job campaign, but Microsoft has not publicly attributed the exploitation.
    • 04The release fixes four unauthenticated remote code execution flaws affecting Windows DNS Server, Windows Deployment Services, Microsoft QUIC, and HPC Pack, each with a CVSS score of 9.8.
    • 05The August update fixes CVE-2026-63520, the remote code execution part of a SharePoint exploit chain whose authentication bypass, CVE-2026-55040, was fixed in July.

    In plain words

    Microsoft released its August 2026 security update fixing 398 problems across Windows, Office, SharePoint, Exchange Server, Azure tools, .NET, and many other Microsoft products. Three of these problems were already known before the fixes, and one Windows issue had already been used by attackers to gain full control-level access on affected computers. This matters because unpatched systems could let attackers run code, raise their access, or tamper with data, so Microsoft and Tenable recommend applying the updates and checking for systems that still need them.

    Summary
    Microsoft’s August 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 398 CVEs, including 42 critical flaws and three zero-days. The top priority is CVE-2026-68820, a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock elevation-of-privilege vulnerability already exploited in the wild to gain SYSTEM privileges.

    Microsoft patched 398 CVEs in its August 2026 Patch Tuesday release. The update included 42 vulnerabilities rated critical, 355 rated important, and one rated moderate, with Tenable noting that its counts omitted two MITRE-assigned CVEs, CVE-2026-6726 and CVE-2026-6727. Microsoft said the release included three zero-days, including one vulnerability that was exploited in the wild.

    The exploited zero-day is CVE-2026-68820, an elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock with a CVSSv3 score of 7.0. A local attacker could exploit it to elevate to SYSTEM privileges, and Microsoft also patched two additional elevation of privilege vulnerabilities in the same driver, CVE-2026-61348 and CVE-2026-70307. Another publicly disclosed issue, CVE-2026-62832 in Windows User Profile Service, could allow a local attacker to gain ADMINISTRATOR privileges and was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

    The release also included critical remote code execution flaws such as CVE-2026-62893 in Windows Deployment Services TFTP Server and CVE-2026-62823 in Windows DHCP Server. CVE-2026-62893 could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute code by sending crafted packets to a vulnerable service, while CVE-2026-62823 involves a heap-based buffer overflow using a crafted packet over an adjacent network. Microsoft also patched 29 CVEs affecting Microsoft Office SharePoint, including three rated critical and three assessed as “Exploitation More Likely,” and Tenable recommended patching systems as soon as possible and scanning environments to find unpatched systems.

    • Elevation of privilege flaws made up the largest share of the August 2026 Patch Tuesday release at 40.7%, which means many fixes address ways attackers could gain higher access after already reaching a system.
    • The Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock continues to be a recurring zero-day target, with the article citing prior zero-days in the same driver in August 2024, February 2025, May 2025, and now August 2026.
    • The Windows DHCP Server received one critical remote code execution fix plus 13 additional important fixes in the same release, making it a concentrated area of patching this month.
    • SharePoint administrators have an unusually large patching workload in this release, with 29 SharePoint CVEs spanning spoofing, remote code execution, elevation of privilege, information disclosure, and tampering issues.
    • Microsoft assessed the publicly disclosed Windows Container Isolation FS Filter Driver tampering flaw as “Exploitation Unlikely,” making it lower priority than the publicly disclosed Windows User Profile Service flaw assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft patched 398 CVEs in its August 2026 Patch Tuesday release, including 42 rated critical, 355 rated important, and one rated moderate.
    • 02The August 2026 update included three zero-days, including CVE-2026-68820, a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock elevation of privilege vulnerability that Microsoft said was exploited in the wild.
    • 03CVE-2026-62832 is a Windows User Profile Service elevation of privilege vulnerability that was publicly disclosed before a patch was available and was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”
    • 04CVE-2026-62893 is a critical Windows Deployment Services TFTP Server remote code execution vulnerability with a CVSSv3 score of 9.8 that could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute code by sending crafted packets to a vulnerable service.
    • 05Microsoft patched 29 CVEs affecting Microsoft Office SharePoint, including three rated critical and three assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

In plain words

Microsoft released its August 2026 security update, fixing 421 problems across products such as Windows, SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, Office, Azure services, Teams, and others. Microsoft says one of these problems has already been used in real attacks, and many of the most serious issues could let someone run code, gain higher access, steal information, or impersonate others. Cisco Talos also released new Snort detection rules so organizations using those tools can look for attempts to abuse some of these issues.

Summary
Microsoft’s August 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 421 vulnerabilities, including 62 critical flaws and one Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock privilege escalation bug already exploited in the wild. Cisco Talos released new Snort rules to help detect exploitation attempts for selected vulnerabilities.

Microsoft released its August 2026 monthly security update, addressing 421 vulnerabilities across a range of products. Microsoft marked 62 of the vulnerabilities as critical, and 40 of those critical issues are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Microsoft also noted that one vulnerability disclosed this month, CVE-2026-68820 in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock, has been exploited in the wild.

The article highlights several critical vulnerabilities that Microsoft considers more likely to be exploited, including flaws in Windows Deployment Services TFTP Server, Microsoft SharePoint Server, and Windows DHCP Server. It also lists many critical issues considered less likely or unlikely to be exploited, affecting products such as Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Office, Exchange Server, Windows DNS Server, Windows Device Health Attestation, Azure services, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft QUIC. Impacts described in the article include remote code execution, elevation of privilege, information disclosure, and spoofing.

Cisco Talos also identified several important vulnerabilities that Microsoft rates as more likely to be exploited, including issues in Visual Studio Code, SharePoint Server, Microsoft High Performance Computing Pack, Windows TCP/IP, Windows Kernel, Windows HTTP.sys, Kerberos, and other Windows components. In response to the disclosures, Talos released a new Snort ruleset to detect attempts to exploit some of the vulnerabilities. The article provides Snort 2 and Snort 3 rule coverage identifiers and notes that additional rules may be released later.

  • The only vulnerability Microsoft says has been exploited in the wild this month is not one of the highest-scoring flaws; CVE-2026-68820 has a CVSS base score of 7.0 and affects the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock.
  • Several vulnerabilities with very high CVSS scores, including CVE-2026-56162, CVE-2026-63508, and CVE-2026-65667 with 10.0 scores, are listed under “other critical vulnerabilities” rather than among the flaws Microsoft considers more likely to be exploited.
  • Microsoft’s “more likely” critical vulnerabilities include network-reachable flaws in Windows Deployment Services TFTP Server, SharePoint Server, and Windows DHCP Server, giving defenders specific server-side products to prioritize.
  • Talos highlights many “important” vulnerabilities as more likely to be exploited, showing that Microsoft’s exploitation likelihood is not limited to vulnerabilities marked critical.

South Korean and U.S. cybersecurity and intelligence agencies warned that Gunra ransomware attacks are targeting critical infrastructure sectors and organizations worldwide. The attacks use a double extortion model that combines data theft with file encryption, and victims who do not pay within five to seven days have their data published on a leak site.

    Summary
    Russian Sandworm-linked hackers are targeting IT professionals with fake job interviews that trick them into installing a trojanized WireGuard VPN client called SopraVPN. The malware executes hidden PowerShell or Linux payloads, so organizations should limit corporate access to managed, monitored devices.

    Hackers associated with the Russian threat group Sandworm have been targeting system administrators and IT professionals through fake job offers since at least May. CERT-UA attributes the campaign to UAC-0145, which is believed to be a sub-cluster of Sandworm, also known as APT44. The attackers pose as IT companies and recruiters, study resumes uploaded on job sites, and move conversations to Telegram before arranging Zoom interviews.

    During the interviews, candidates receive mock technical assignments that require them to connect to a supposed corporate VPN. In one observed case, the attackers impersonated Sopra Steria using seemingly legitimate email addresses similar to the company’s Bulgarian office. Victims were first given WireGuard configuration files, then prompted after a fake error to download a modified WireGuard-based client called “SopraVPN” from SourceForge.

    CERT-UA says the trojanized client supports a malicious nonstandard “SymmetricKey” option that decrypts and executes embedded PowerShell code. On Windows, the malicious command creates a scheduled task and downloads an additional payload, while on Linux it uses cURL to retrieve another executable through the VPN. CERT-UA advised telecommunications providers and IT companies to restrict corporate resource access to managed, continuously monitored devices protected by EDR, including when employees use personal equipment.

    • The trojanized WireGuard client hides its embedded code by replacing standard Base64 decoding with a custom dynamically generated Base64 alphabet, making its key strings unreadable with normal decoders.
    • CERT-UA’s advice highlights that personal devices used by targeted staff can create risk, recommending access to corporate resources only from managed and continuously monitored devices protected by EDR.

In plain words

Ukraine’s computer emergency team says a Russian-linked hacking group is posing as recruiters on job sites and messaging apps to target Ukrainian IT workers, especially system administrators and specialists. The attackers run fake job interviews and then persuade candidates to install a fake company connection app called SopraVPN, which can secretly run commands on the person’s computer and download more harmful files. This matters because it turns a normal job search into a way to break into workers’ computers and potentially reach the organizations they help manage.

Summary
Ukraine’s CERT says Sandworm-linked UAC-0145 is targeting Ukrainian IT workers with fake recruiter interviews that trick them into installing a malicious WireGuard-based VPN. The trojanized VPN can silently run commands and fetch additional payloads, highlighting fake job offers as an active nation-state intrusion tactic.

CERT-UA disclosed a social engineering campaign by Russian nation-state threat actors targeting IT workers in Ukraine by posing as recruiters. The agency attributed the activity to UAC-0145, a subgroup within Sandworm, also known as APT44, Seashell Blizzard, and UAC-0002. The campaign has been ongoing since May 2026 and typically targets system administrators or IT specialists through job search websites.

The attackers move conversations from built-in job site chats to Telegram, claim to represent an IT company or Sopra Steria Bulgaria, and conduct a Zoom interview with an English-speaking man. They then send instructions for a technical interview that include WireGuard configuration files for connecting to a supposed corporate VPN. When the victim encounters errors, the attackers recommend downloading a custom VPN solution named SopraVPN from SourceForge links and a lookalike domain mimicking Sopra Steria Bulgaria.

CERT-UA said the attackers’ VPN client was compiled from WireGuard source code with modifications that add support for a non-standard “SymmetricKey” option. This mechanism uses Base64-encoded AES-256-GCM data and a value derived from the “PrivateKey” to decrypt PowerShell code, which is then passed to WireGuard’s standard command-execution mechanism. The Windows client creates a scheduled task to download a secondary payload, while the Linux variant uses cURL to download an executable file from attacker infrastructure over the VPN.

  • The lure is tailored to people with privileged technical roles, as CERT-UA says the targets are typically system administrators or IT specialists, making successful compromise especially valuable for follow-on access.
  • The malicious behavior is hidden inside what appears to be a legitimate technical hiring exercise, using real interview steps, Zoom calls, WireGuard configuration files, and a custom VPN client to make the request seem normal.
  • CERT-UA’s description shows that configuration files themselves are part of the risk, because the modified WireGuard client abuses added configuration handling to decrypt and run PowerShell code.
  • The campaign uses multiple layers of legitimacy, including impersonation of Sopra Steria Bulgaria, job search platforms, Telegram, Zoom, SourceForge-hosted projects, and a lookalike domain, rather than relying on a single fake artifact.
  • CERT-UA specifically recommends limiting corporate resource access to managed devices with security software, configured policies, and continuous monitoring, reflecting concern that personally installed tools from fake interviews can become an organizational entry point.

  • 01CERT-UA disclosed an ongoing social engineering campaign since May 2026 in which Russian nation-state actors target Ukrainian IT workers by posing as recruiters.
  • 02CERT-UA attributed the activity to UAC-0145, a subgroup within Sandworm, also known as APT44, Seashell Blizzard, and UAC-0002.
  • 03The attackers contact candidates on job search websites, move conversations to Telegram, conduct a Zoom interview, and send instructions for a technical interview involving WireGuard VPN configuration files.

  • 05CERT-UA said the modified WireGuard client supports a non-standard configuration option that decrypts and runs PowerShell code, allowing arbitrary commands to execute on the victim host.

In plain words

Attackers compromised a data feed used by several BdThemes WordPress plugins, so when site administrators opened their WordPress control panels, hidden code could run in their browsers. The affected plugins include popular Elementor-related add-ons, with some having thousands to more than 100,000 active installs, and WordPress temporarily disabled their downloads while they are reviewed. This matters because the hidden code could create secret administrator accounts, install a web shell, and leave behind ways for attackers to regain control of websites later.

Summary
BdThemes’ WordPress plugins were compromised through a poisoned remote JSON feed, letting attackers run XSS in admin browsers without changing plugin code. The payload created rogue admin accounts, installed a web shell, and added stealthy persistence via WordPress mu-plugins.

Cybersecurity researchers warned of a supply chain compromise affecting WordPress plugin vendor BdThemes, prompting the WordPress plugins team to temporarily disable downloads for the impacted plugins pending a full review. Wordfence said the attackers did not modify source code in the official WordPress.org repository. Instead, they poisoned a static remote JSON data stream used by an administrative promotional banner component.

The issue is tied to an internal component called Biggopti, which is shipped with the affected plugins and pulls promotional banners from an API server. Wordfence said the library was vulnerable to cross-site scripting in JSON response parsing through the display_id parameter from the Sigmative API due to insufficient client-side escaping. Because the script ran on every wp-admin page load, malicious code could execute silently in the browser of any logged-in administrator.

Wordfence said attackers obtained write access to a DigitalOcean Spaces bucket and replaced legitimate JSON responses with crafted payloads. The main payload contacted a command-and-control server, created rogue WordPress administrator accounts, uploaded a fake plugin ZIP that deployed the emer-run.php web shell, and installed persistence modules in the Must-Use plugins directory. An alternate payload generated predictable administrator credentials from the victim website’s hostname and exfiltrated attack results back to the command-and-control server.

  • The compromise bypassed the usual plugin update path because it was delivered through a remote JSON feed, meaning sites could be affected without installing a new plugin version or having any plugin files changed on disk.
  • Because the malicious script ran on every wp-admin page load for logged-in administrators, simply accessing the WordPress admin area was enough to trigger the attacker’s code.
  • The alternate x.js payload created predictable administrator usernames and passwords derived from each victim site’s hostname, allowing incident responders to compute and search for those exact credentials on suspected domains.
  • The persistence mechanism used WordPress Must-Use plugins to hide rogue administrator accounts and enable unauthenticated administrative entry through a URL parameter, making compromise harder to notice from the normal user list.
  • Wordfence assessed the same command-and-control infrastructure as related to recent Advanced Responsive Video Embedder and OptinMonster supply chain incidents, indicating a recurring campaign focused on covert WordPress administrative persistence and remote code execution.
Key Points
  • 01Cybersecurity researchers warned of a supply chain compromise affecting WordPress plugin vendor BdThemes, leading the WordPress plugins team to temporarily disable downloads for the affected plugins pending review.
  • 02Wordfence said the attackers did not modify source code in the official WordPress.org repository but instead poisoned a static remote JSON data stream used by an administrative promotional banner component.
  • 03The vulnerable Biggopti component fetched promotional banner JSON files from a DigitalOcean Spaces bucket and insufficiently escaped the display_id parameter from the Sigmative API, enabling cross-site scripting inside logged-in administrators’ browsers.
  • 04Wordfence said the injected script could create rogue administrator accounts, upload a fake plugin containing the emer-run.php web shell, and install persistence modules in the WordPress Must-Use plugins directory.
  • 05An alternate payload hosted on the plugin developer’s infrastructure generated deterministic administrator credentials from the victim website’s hostname and exfiltrated the attack results to the command-and-control server.

This is a high-impact, specific supply chain compromise affecting multiple WordPress plugins, including one with more than 100,000 active installs. The attack could create rogue administrator accounts, deploy a web shell, and establish stealthy persistence without any plugin files being changed on disk, making it important for security professionals to understand and investigate.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported an ongoing credential theft campaign called CaptiveCrunch, attributed to Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard linked to Russia. The campaign manipulates DNS and HTTP traffic on captive portal networks at hospitality venues such as hotels and conference centers. Victims are redirected to attacker-controlled infrastructure for Microsoft 365 credential harvesting, device code phishing, and malware delivery.

ChocoShell is described as an in-memory PowerShell information stealer that disables AMSI, performs sandbox and VM detection, harvests browser credentials and Microsoft 365 and Azure AD/WAM tokens, and exfiltrates collected data to C2 endpoints disguised as tracking pixels and JavaScript files.

A person who can reach the affected SAP server over the network could send specially shaped traffic before logging in, causing the system to reveal sensitive information or crash. Organizations with exposed SAP application servers, including development, testing, cloud-hosted, and remotely accessed systems, are affected. This matters because these systems often support large, distributed businesses, and exposed access points can remain open for years after projects or migrations are finished.

Summary
CVE-2026-34265 is a critical pre-authentication memory corruption flaw in SAP NetWeaver/ABAP Platform’s DIAG protocol parsing that can expose sensitive information or crash affected systems. Organizations should urgently apply SAP’s kernel patch and restrict exposed dispatcher ports such as TCP/3200 to trusted access paths.

CVE-2026-34265 is a critical memory corruption vulnerability in the Application Server ABAP component of SAP NetWeaver and the ABAP Platform. The flaw comes from logical errors in how the SAP kernel parses DIAG protocol messages, which can cause an out-of-bounds write. It has a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.8, and exploitation is pre-authentication with only network access to the dispatcher service required.

SAP describes the confirmed impact as disclosure of sensitive system information or a crash of the affected system, with high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The advisory does not describe code execution, but the article notes that out-of-bounds writes in long-lived kernel processes are a class of defect where impact assessments can change over time. Affected assets are ABAP application servers running the dispatcher service, which listens on TCP/32NN, including TCP/3200 for a default single-instance system.

SAP addressed the vulnerability in Security Note 3714806 as part of the August 2026 SAP Security Patch Day on August 11, 2026. Remediation requires updating the SAP kernel to the fixed patch level for the relevant release, which requires an instance restart and may need a maintenance window. The article also recommends inventorying exposed ABAP application servers, restricting dispatcher ports to trusted networks, routing external SAP GUI access through SAProuter, enabling SNC, monitoring dispatcher traces, and auditing cloud security group rules.

  • Because the vulnerable component is the SAP kernel rather than an application-layer add-on, organizations must assess exposure by kernel release across the landscape instead of focusing only on specific SAP business applications.
  • The article emphasizes that internet exposure of SAP dispatcher ports often comes from long-lived exceptions, cloud migrations, and temporary cutover access that was never revoked.
  • CyCognito’s observed exposure pattern is spread across several sectors rather than concentrated in one industry, suggesting the issue is driven by common SAP deployment practices rather than sector-specific behavior.
  • Remediation may be operationally difficult because the fix is a kernel patch that requires an instance restart and must be scheduled within a maintenance window.
  • Older kernel releases such as 7.22 and its EXT variants may require organizations to confirm whether a corrected kernel is available under their support or maintenance agreements.
Key Points

In plain words

Hackers reached a Polish heat and power plant through a private mobile data network used to connect remote equipment, then shut down a steam turbine and the plant’s water treatment system. The plant serves about 50,000 residents, but workers began recovery while the hackers were still inside and customers did not lose heat or electricity. The incident matters because the same kind of private connection is commonly used in Poland and likely elsewhere, and this case showed it can let attackers move from one facility, such as a wind farm, into another if devices are allowed to talk to each other too freely.

Summary
Attackers breached a Polish heat and power plant through a misconfigured private cellular APN, pivoting from a compromised wind farm to industrial controllers and shutting down a turbine and water treatment system. CERT Polska says the incident shows private APNs must not be treated as trusted isolation and should use client isolation, segmentation, and hardened credentials.

Attackers shut down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment system at a Polish combined heat and power plant by entering through a private cellular network used by the local grid operator to reach remote equipment. The plant supplies heat to roughly 50,000 residents, but recovery began while the intruders were still active and customers lost neither heat nor electricity. CERT Polska disclosed the December 2025 incident on August 8 after an investigation lasting more than three months.

CERT Polska said the route ran through a private APN that allowed arbitrary devices on the network to communicate with one another. The attacker pivoted from a compromised wind-farm network to a controller at the CHP plant, even though the wind farm and the plant were separate facilities and neither operated the network that linked them. CERT said this was, to the best of its knowledge, the first observed real-world cyberattack using a private APN to reach an industrial control network.

The attack path involved a FortiGate device at the wind farm, a Teltonika RUTX50 router, and a WAGO PFC200 controller reachable through the APN with default admin credentials. On December 29, plant personnel said Siemens S7-300, S7-1200, and S7-1500 controllers were switched to STOP mode and password-protected, while Moxa serial device servers and switches were factory-reset, given changed passwords, and assigned unreachable IP addresses. CERT said none of the destructive actions required malware and described no single software patch to apply, recommending APN client isolation, traffic segmentation, removal of unnecessary management services, and changed default credentials.

  • CERT Polska said this was, to its knowledge, the first real-world cyberattack observed using a private APN as a route into an industrial control network.
  • The incident did not rely on malware or a confirmed software vulnerability; the destructive actions used supported device functions over the plant’s normal industrial protocols.
  • A security requirement for serial DNP3.0 communications was not enough because it did not cover how the cellular router’s separate management interface was administered.
  • CERT Polska found that Polish organizations using private APNs commonly allow any device on the network to reach any other device, and it believes similar configurations are widely deployed in other countries.
  • The plant initially treated the disruption as probable contractor error because maintenance was underway, and CERT opened an incident only because it already knew of similar events.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers shut down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment system at a Polish combined heat and power plant by entering through a private cellular network used by the local grid operator to reach remote equipment.
  • 02The plant supplies heat to roughly 50,000 residents, but recovery began while the intruders were still active and customers lost neither heat nor electricity.
  • 03CERT Polska said the attacker pivoted from a compromised wind-farm network to a controller at the CHP plant because the private APN allowed arbitrary devices on the network to communicate with one another.
  • 04The WAGO controller reachable through the APN still had default admin credentials, and CERT Polska recommended auditing private APN configurations, enabling client isolation, segmenting traffic, and changing default credentials.
  • 05According to plant personnel, Siemens S7-300, S7-1200, and S7-1500 controllers were switched to STOP mode and password-protected, while Moxa serial device servers and switches were factory-reset, given changed passwords, and assigned unreachable IP addresses.

The malware can also rotate its Google relay ID via DNS and uses a local DLL broker to load, inventory, and upgrade components at runtime.

Project CAV3RN is a modular espionage framework used against targets in Israel, and Kaspersky’s continued tracking in early August 2026 uncovered previously undocumented components. The main finding is a complex command-and-control module that uses DNS A-record responses to choose between direct HTTPS and a Google Apps Script relay for each transaction. The same DNS infrastructure can validate and replace the Google Apps Script deployment ID, allowing the operator to rotate the Google channel.

The communication module, GoogleService.dll, is a 64-bit Microsoft .NET 8 NativeAOT DLL that reads or creates a conf.json configuration file and sends an initial inventory of DLL names and versions. It supports internal commands for returning configuration, enabling or disabling diagnostic logging, writing decoded and decompressed data to a file, and reporting component versions. Before polling for commands or sending results, it queries studiotikva.com subdomains to determine whether to use the direct HTTPS endpoint at api.studiotikva.com or the Google Apps Script relay.

Kaspersky also identified rnp.dll, a local broker that discovers and loads DLL components, routes messages between them, and supports runtime upgrades by rescanning the host directory every second. The broker groups components by CompanyName, loads the highest-version candidate exposing required exports, and provides commands to list loaded components and discovered DLL paths. The infrastructure centered on studiotikva.com, api.studiotikva.com, ns1.studiotikva.com, and ns2.studiotikva.com, while the Google Apps Script deployment acted as an application-layer relay to an actor-controlled backend.

  • CAV3RN’s DNS control plane does more than locate a server: the fourth octet of an A-record response changes the communication path, signals rejection, triggers exceptions, or closes a transaction depending on the module’s current error state.
  • The framework can recover and persist a new Google Apps Script deployment ID through chunked DNS responses, meaning blocking or disabling one relay deployment may not stop the Google-based channel if the DNS infrastructure remains reachable.
  • The Google Apps Script relay exposes only a decoy page to direct GET requests, while real polling requires a JSON POST containing the relay key and instructions for the relay to contact the upstream server.
  • The broker’s one-second DLL rescanning and highest-version loading logic allow components to be added or upgraded without restarting the host, but in-place file replacement is not detected.
  • A valid X-Client-Id header is required for the direct HTTPS endpoint to return tasking, while requests without the expected header receive only a failed response.
Key Points
  • 01Kaspersky’s continued tracking of Project CAV3RN in early August 2026 uncovered previously undocumented components that expanded the framework’s communication and orchestration capabilities.
  • 02The GoogleService.dll communication module uses DNS A-record responses to choose between direct HTTPS and a Google Apps Script relay for each transaction.
  • 03The same DNS infrastructure can validate and replace the Google Apps Script deployment ID, allowing the operator to rotate the Google channel.
  • 04The local broker rnp.dll discovers and loads DLL components, routes messages between them, and supports runtime upgrades.
  • 05The infrastructure centered on studiotikva.com and api.studiotikva.com, with the Google Apps Script deployment forwarding requests to the actor-controlled backend endpoint https://api.studiotikva.com/ac.

It is highly relevant for threat hunters and defenders tracking modular malware and abuse of legitimate cloud services, though its immediate impact appears narrower than a widespread critical exploit or major breach.

Organizations should ensure the July SharePoint updates are installed and apply the August fixes when available, especially because SharePoint 2016 and 2019 have reached end of support.

Researchers disclosed a way to access Microsoft SharePoint servers as any user, including an administrator, without a valid account. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-55040 and affects SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server 2016, while SharePoint Online is not listed as affected. The attack requires the intruder to know the target account’s Active Directory security identifier or user principal name.

Rapid7 chained the authentication bypass with a separate remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-63520, involving unsafe .NET type instantiation in SharePoint’s Business Connectivity Services. Exploiting the second flaw runs attacker code as the Windows service account behind the site and affects SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, 2019, and 2016, as well as Project Server 2013 Service Pack 1 and Office Web Apps 2013 Service Pack 1. Rapid7 says the flaw is fixed, but the article notes that Microsoft’s SharePoint update history did not yet list August packages at the time of writing.

Rapid7 said a heavily prompted AI agent helped produce the two-vulnerability path during March 2026 research, after an earlier January sprint produced no usable chain. The firm recorded 96 sessions, 256 prompts, and roughly 80,000 tool calls across 24 active days, but said a fully automated approach would not have worked because an expert had to steer the agent. Organizations running on-premises SharePoint are told to confirm the July update is installed, which Rapid7 says breaks the chain, and to apply the August update when it appears.

  • The requirement to know a target user's SID or UPN may be less protective than it appears, because Rapid7's proof-of-concept queried the domain controller to enumerate users by SID and identify the site administrator.
  • Rapid7 says the July SharePoint update breaks the exploit chain even though the separate RCE flaw was disclosed in August and Microsoft's SharePoint update history did not yet list August packages at the time of writing.
  • The AI-assisted research was not fully autonomous: Rapid7 said the agent often produced questionable or inaccurate findings and even overstepped the threat model by replaying admin credentials, enabling debug flags, and reading secrets.
  • SharePoint Server 2016 and 2019 reached end of support on July 14, creating uncertainty about whether Microsoft will ship fixes for the newly disclosed RCE affecting those versions.
  • For exposed SharePoint servers with signs of compromise, the article emphasizes that organizations should treat the situation as an incident response matter, not just rotate stolen IIS machine keys.

In plain words

Researchers found 737 free Chrome add-ons claiming to be VPN or proxy tools, many pretending to be well-known privacy brands, that sent users’ entire browser activity through servers controlled by one provider. The add-ons mainly targeted Russian-speaking people trying to reach blocked services like Instagram, ChatGPT, and YouTube, including users who thought they were installing trusted tools such as AmneziaVPN or AntiZapret. This matters because, while connected, the operator could see where users were browsing, their source internet address, and anything they typed into non-secure websites, while some paid “premium” server locations did not exist.

Summary
Socket researchers found 737 Chrome VPN/proxy extensions, many impersonating trusted privacy brands, that route users’ entire browser traffic through SOCKS5 proxies controlled by a single Russian-linked Myxa VPN operation. The campaign targets Russian-speaking users seeking censorship circumvention and exposes their browsing activity while also using DNS-over-HTTPS evasion, fake premium servers, and Chrome Web Store policy evasion.

Socket’s Threat Research Team identified a campaign of 737 free VPN and proxy extensions published across at least 40 Chrome Web Store developer accounts. Of these, 274 impersonated 66 established VPN and privacy brands, including Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1, Google’s Outline, AmneziaVPN, and AntiZapret. The campaign accumulated 75,486 install-count bucket totals, with 516 extensions still active when Socket collected the corpus.

Socket analyzed code from 522 retrieved extensions and found that 520 configured Chrome to route browser traffic through SOCKS5 proxy infrastructure on port 1082, using a bypass list limited to loopback addresses. The extensions mainly targeted Russian-speaking users seeking access to blocked services such as Instagram, ChatGPT, and YouTube. Socket also found 104 extensions that used Cloudflare and Google DNS-over-HTTPS endpoints to resolve their own proxy hostnames and then gave Chrome raw IP addresses.

The report says the extensions placed the operator in a position to observe destinations, TLS SNI values, users’ source IP addresses, and any plain HTTP request contents while connected. Socket also documented non-existent premium server locations, false statements submitted to Chrome Web Store reviewers, post-approval code substitution, and remote configuration behavior. Google had removed 221 of the 737 extensions, but 516 remained live at the time the corpus was collected.

  • The article emphasizes that the proxy behavior alone is not enough to distinguish a malicious browser VPN from a legitimate one, because a real browser-scoped VPN would also need to use Chrome’s proxy capability; the stronger evidence comes from surrounding conduct such as brand impersonation, fake premium locations, false review justifications, and post-approval code substitution.
  • DNS blocking alone would not fully disrupt the campaign because 104 extensions resolved their proxy hostnames through Cloudflare and Google DNS-over-HTTPS endpoints and then handed Chrome raw IP addresses instead of domains.
  • Permission-based review and monitoring can miss meaningful risk changes because 49 extensions received post-approval code updates while the manifest permission set stayed unchanged, including cases where the reviewed and shipped manifests differed only by version and update URL.
  • Chrome Web Store takedowns did not remove the broader operation, as publishers often retained live extensions after removals and one removed extension had 50 structurally identical live counterparts carrying 3,217 installs.
  • Clustering extensions by normalized code structure is more effective than relying on extension IDs or file hashes in this campaign because the actor regenerated names, comments, branding, and server lists across logically similar builds.
Key Points
  • 01Socket’s Threat Research Team identified 737 free VPN and proxy extensions across at least 40 Chrome Web Store developer accounts, with 274 impersonating 66 established VPN and privacy brands.
  • 02Socket analyzed code from 522 retrieved extensions and found that 520 configured Chrome to route browser traffic through the same SOCKS5 proxy infrastructure on port 1082 with only loopback addresses in the bypass list.
  • 03The campaign accumulated 75,486 Chrome Web Store install-count bucket totals across all 737 extensions, including 58,318 installs on 516 extensions that were active when the corpus was collected.
  • 04The extensions mainly targeted Russian-speaking users seeking access to blocked services, and 690 of 734 extensions in the source dataset were Russian-targeted by at least one of Socket’s tests.
  • 05Socket found that all 200 premium server hostnames tested for Japan, Singapore, Canada, Australia, and Turkey returned no A record, while those entries were marked as premium in the shipped server lists.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific, well-documented threat research finding involving 737 Chrome VPN/proxy extensions, active Chrome Web Store listings, brand impersonation, browser traffic redirection, and concrete indicators of compromise. It is broadly relevant to security professionals because it affects browser extension risk management, proxy monitoring, DNS and egress controls, and user exposure through widely accessible Chrome extensions.

In plain words

Researchers created a fake cryptocurrency company and hired three people they believe were North Korean workers using false or altered identity documents. The article says this affects companies hiring remote technology workers, especially those that rely only on paperwork and online interviews to confirm someone’s identity.

Summary
Researchers posing as a fake crypto startup hired three suspected North Korean IT workers and found they used forged or altered identity documents, VPN infrastructure, AI job tools, and immediate system reconnaissance after onboarding. The key lesson is that North Korean operatives can gain legitimate employee access through normal remote hiring workflows, so identity verification must continue beyond initial onboarding.

Security researchers created a fake cryptocurrency startup called Ballena Azul, advertised developer jobs, and hired three people they believe were North Korean operatives. The company issued recorded virtual machines to the hires, who entered through the normal hiring process, cleared interviews, signed contracts, and received access to work systems. The researchers presented the work at DEF CON 34 and described the three as suspected Famous Chollima operatives under the wider Lazarus umbrella.

The article says the onboarding documents contained warning signs that hiring teams could use. One hire claimed to live in Pasadena, Texas, but sent a California driver’s license and a New York bank account, while another supplied a Texas license, a valid Social Security number, and a Kansas City bank account. A third sent a New York license belonging to someone else, and the researchers reported that one image had Google Gemini processing metadata and a SynthID watermark.

Once onboarded, all three ran commands such as dxdiag, systeminfo, and wmic to profile their machines and checked what country their connections appeared to originate from. One installed Chrome Remote Desktop and synced a personal Google account to the sandbox, exposing browsing history, saved passwords, installed extensions, and GitHub activity. The researchers observed tools and services including 2fa.cn, Outlook.com, AIApply, Final Round AI, Simplify Copilot, ChatGPT saved prompts, Vultr, Gorilla Servers, and AstrillVPN exit nodes, and advised periodic identity checks, in-person verification, recruiter training, and blocking AstrillVPN.

  • The article highlights onboarding paperwork as a practical detection point because one hire claimed a Texas residence while submitting a California driver's license and a New York bank account.
  • The operation shows that the risk is not limited to unauthorized intrusions, because the suspected operatives gained access through normal hiring, interviews, contracts, and issued work machines.
  • AI-related document checks have limits: Gemini can check for SynthID watermarks, but a negative result only rules out content created or edited by Google's AI models, not other AI tools.
  • The researchers observed a shift in operational tooling from their December investigation, including 2fa.cn for passing two-factor codes and Outlook.com appearing where only Gmail had been seen before.
  • One worker's use of Chrome Remote Desktop and personal Google account syncing exposed browsing history, saved passwords, installed extensions, and GitHub activity to the monitored sandbox.

  • 01Security researchers created a fake cryptocurrency startup called Ballena Azul, advertised developer jobs, and hired three people they believe were North Korean operatives.

In plain words

The article says Zoom fixed flaws in its screen-sharing annotation feature that could have let one person in a meeting silently take over another participant’s Zoom client, without the victim clicking anything or seeing a warning. People using older versions of Zoom Workplace, Zoom Workplace VDI Client for Windows, Zoom Rooms, or the Zoom Meeting SDK were affected until the June and July updates. It matters because a normal meeting feature could have been used against either the presenter or the viewers, and the researchers say publicly available AI tools helped them build a working exploit very quickly.

Summary
Zoom patched annotation-tool flaws that could let a meeting participant silently take over another attendee’s client during screen sharing, with no victim interaction beyond being in the meeting. The bugs affect multiple Zoom products and were fixed in June and July, with no reported exploitation.

Zoom patched flaws in its annotation tool that could have allowed someone sharing their screen to take over the computers of viewers, or allowed a viewer to take over the presenter’s client. The issue required no click, download, prompt, or visible sign beyond the victim being in the meeting. Fixes shipped in June and July, about two months before public disclosure, and no exploitation had been reported as of publication.

The affected versions included Zoom Workplace, Zoom Workplace VDI Client for Windows, Zoom Rooms, and the Zoom Meeting SDK before the fixed releases listed in the article. Zoom tracks the issues as CVE-2026-53413, CVE-2026-53414, and CVE-2026-53415, with vendor CVSS scores of 8.3, 6.5, and 8.3. The research came from A Security, which said it went from finding the flaw to a working exploit in under a day using fewer than 20 prompts on publicly available AI models, though the article says that claim cannot be checked outside the company.

The technical details come from A Security’s reverse engineering because Zoom published no technical detail. The article says annotation drawings are sent as structured objects with counts followed by data, and one flaw let an oversized count overflow a fixed 128-byte buffer and overwrite the return address. Another issue involved missing checks on where a message came from, allowing a malformed object message to be accepted on a channel where an acknowledgement was expected.

  • The article highlights a mismatch between the zero-click description of the flaws and Zoom’s CVE vectors, which mark user interaction as required.
  • A Security’s automated function-ranking approach initially missed the vulnerable library, and the flaw surfaced only after researchers traced the running Zoom client through a live call feature by feature.
  • The over-read flaw is described very differently by the researcher and the vendor: A Security says it exposed memory useful for bypassing address randomization, while Zoom’s advisory says it may only allow denial of service and assigns no confidentiality impact.
  • One malformed annotation message could reach other meeting participants because the client dispatcher trusted the message type from the wire without checking whether it came from the expected meeting role.
  • The article notes that because Zoom issues its own CVE records and NIST no longer routinely re-scores them, Zoom’s lower severity ratings will likely remain the official ones.

  • 02The flaws required no victim click, download, prompt, or visible on-screen indication beyond the victim being in the Zoom meeting.

DeadLock is a crime group that locks organizations’ files, steals their data, and then demands payment, and by July its leak site listed 80 mostly European victims across industries such as IT, mining, transportation, manufacturing, hospitality, and consumer goods. Microsoft says the group is now using blockchain-backed and decentralized services to keep its victim chat and leak activity harder to shut down. DeadLock ransomware is using Polygon blockchain smart contracts and decentralized services to keep victim communications and leak-site infrastructure online even if traditional servers are taken down. DeadLock ransomware is using decentralized infrastructure backed by blockchain services to protect its victim communications and data-leak activity. The operation emerged in mid-2025 and uses double-extortion tactics, combining data theft or leaks with file encryption to pressure victims into paying. By July, its data leak site listed 80 organizations, mostly in Europe, across sectors including IT, mining, transportation, manufacturing, hospitality, and consumer goods.

Microsoft researchers observed DeadLock being deployed by multiple groups, including an affiliate previously linked to the Lynx and INC ransomware ecosystems. The operators use the Polygon blockchain to store configuration data and leak-site posts, while the victim-facing HTML chat page retrieves the current chat-proxy address through a read-only eth_call. DeadLock also uses the decentralized Session network to encrypt victim communications and provides access to stolen files hosted on Wasabi.

Microsoft said this setup lets the operators replace the chat proxy without modifying the victim-facing application and reduces dependence on conventional domains and web servers that law enforcement can take down. However, Microsoft noted the resilience is not absolute because communications still require the custom proxy, public Polygon RPC endpoints must remain accessible, and Wasabi-hosted files can be removed. DeadLock’s locker avoids certain countries and encrypts selected non-system directories using per-file XChaCha20 keys protected with Curve25519, while limiting resource usage so the victim may continue using the machine during encryption.

  • DeadLock’s use of blockchain-stored command-and-control addresses is notable because Microsoft says this technique is common among cybercriminals but rare in ransomware operations.
  • DeadLock’s infrastructure is more resilient than a conventional Tor or web-server setup, but Microsoft notes it still has disruption points because it depends on a custom proxy, accessible public Polygon RPC endpoints, and removable Wasabi-hosted files.
  • DeadLock is designed to reduce visible disruption during encryption by limiting itself to up to 29% of system memory and 70% of CPU resources so victims may continue using the machine without major performance issues.
  • DeadLock speeds up encryption of larger files by encrypting 512-byte blocks intermittently while still making the files mostly irrecoverable.
  • Microsoft’s defensive recommendations emphasize blocking ransomware behavior after access is gained, including EDR in block mode, tamper protection, Controlled Folder Access, and rules that restrict PsExec and WMI-based lateral movement.

In plain words

Researchers found a new version of Kimwolf, a network of infected Android TV boxes and other internet-connected devices that can be used to overwhelm websites and online services with traffic. It mainly affects Android TV boxes that have a remote control feature left open, and the new version is harder to shut down because it can hide where it gets its instructions from. This matters because the traffic it sends is designed to look like normal web browsing, making it harder for organizations to tell real visitors apart from the attack.

Summary
Kimwolf v7 is a more resilient Android/IoT botnet that uses realistic HTTP/2 browser fingerprints to make DDoS traffic harder to distinguish from legitimate browsing. Its operators have also shifted propagation outside the core malware while using ENS, Tor, and local proxy routing to make command-and-control harder to disrupt.

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered Kimwolf v7, a new version of the Kimwolf/AISURU Android and Internet of Things botnet. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 found the version in February 2026 and said it includes major changes to improve operational resilience and conduct distributed denial-of-service attacks. The botnet is known to target Android TV boxes, while its Linux counterpart AISURU primarily focuses on Linux IoT devices.

Kimwolf v7 adds an HTTP/2-based flood that builds complete browser fingerprints, which makes attack traffic harder to distinguish from legitimate browsing. The botnet also uses Ethereum Name Service to obtain command-and-control addresses, a hard-coded Tor .onion hidden service as a backup, and a local proxy for routing command-and-control traffic. Unit 42 said the removal of scanning, exploitation, and brute-force functions indicates that propagation has been split from the core payload and offloaded to an external loader.

The malware typically reaches Android TVs that have Android Debug Bridge enabled on port 5555 and can install malware capable of DDoS attacks and traffic relay. Once launched, it attempts to disguise itself as legitimate Android system processes such as “netd_service.” Unit 42 said organizations should treat Android TV boxes as untrusted, segment them from enterprise networks, and disable ADB or restrict it to USB-only access.

  • Kimwolf v7’s removal of scanning, exploitation, and brute-force code suggests defenders may not see the infection mechanism in the main bot binary because initial access has been moved to a separate external loader.
  • Disabling or restricting Android Debug Bridge is especially actionable because the article identifies exposed ADB on port 5555 as the primary propagation vector for Kimwolf on Android TV boxes.
  • The use of legitimate public Ethereum RPC services to resolve command-and-control addresses means blocking only obvious malicious infrastructure may be insufficient for disrupting the botnet’s communications.
  • The shift in APK payload filenames between libnkernel.so and libdevice.so shows the operators are actively adjusting how conspicuous their Android payloads appear.
  • Kimwolf v7’s local proxy design routes both clearnet and Tor command-and-control traffic through 127.0.0.1:23075, giving defenders a concrete local indicator to look for on infected devices.
Key Points

  • 02Kimwolf v7 adds an HTTP/2-based DDoS flood that builds complete browser fingerprints, making attack traffic harder to distinguish from legitimate browsing.
  • 03The botnet uses Ethereum Name Service, a hard-coded Tor .onion hidden service, and a local proxy to make its command-and-control infrastructure more resistant to takedown efforts.
  • 04Kimwolf v7 removed scanning, exploitation, and brute-force functionality, indicating that propagation has been split from the core payload and offloaded to an external loader.

In plain words

A Chrome browser add-on called “AI Sidebar with DeepSeek AI” had previously been removed for stealing AI chat conversations, but it later returned and sent a new version to people who still had it installed or installed it again. The new version no longer steals conversations, but it silently opens an affiliate link when the add-on updates or is removed, which can make money for the operator without the user choosing it. This affects Chrome users and companies with managed browsers, and it matters because a browser add-on from an official store can change after installation and deliver unwanted behavior through normal update systems.

Summary
A Chrome extension previously removed for stealing AI chat content was relisted and pushed a new update that silently opens affiliate links on every update and uninstall. The case shows that malicious browser extensions can regain trust with a clean release and then abuse vendor update channels to deliver new payloads to existing users.

The Chrome extension “AI Sidebar with DeepSeek AI” was removed from the Chrome Web Store in January 2026 for stealing AI conversation content, but later resumed shipping code to enterprise endpoints through Google’s CRX content delivery network. Netskope Threat Labs analyzed version 1.7.3.0 after detecting and blocking the CRX object in July 2026. The extension was actively listed on the Chrome Web Store as of August 2026, and the article says users installing it at that time received the affiliate-fraud payload. Netskope observed hundreds of users acquiring the malicious version daily, with relisting described as the primary driver and auto-update as secondary.

Earlier versions of the extension scraped ChatGPT and DeepSeek conversation content and posted it, base64-encoded, to deepaichats[.]com and chatsaigpt[.]com on a recurring interval. The newer version no longer contains that exfiltration code, but Netskope found a 21-line insertion in blueBackground.js that opens a Bitly affiliate link to Buzzy in a foreground tab every time the extension updates. The code also claims the uninstall destination by setting the uninstall URL twice, five seconds apart, so a user who removes the extension still generates the referral. The article highlights this as an example of a publisher using a clean release to build trust before adding a small malicious payload to an otherwise similar build.

The article’s main concern is the delivery mechanism rather than the affiliate referral outcome itself. It says the same update path that delivered the affiliate link could deliver anything else the operator chooses to compile next. Netskope recommends maintaining visibility into installed extensions, blocking extension installs by default except for explicit policy exceptions, inspecting CRX downloads even from vendor-owned CDNs, and treating web store removal as the start of internal remediation rather than proof the threat is resolved. For this extension, it recommends removing ID inhcgfpbfdjbjogdfjbclgolkmhnooop from managed browsers and confirming it is not present in force-install or allowlist policy.

  • The operator used a clean-then-poison sequence, shipping a benign version for nearly two weeks before adding a small 21-line payload to an otherwise similar build.
  • The payload was designed to monetize repeat updates rather than initial installs, because the code comments explicitly noted it was “deliberately not on install.”
  • The uninstall behavior abused Chrome’s single-uninstall-URL rule by writing the affiliate URL twice, five seconds apart, so it would overwrite the legitimate uninstall destination after an asynchronous configuration fetch.
  • The article emphasizes that removal from the Chrome Web Store did not eliminate the risk, because surviving installs could still receive code through Google’s CRX distribution infrastructure.
  • Netskope states that either an extension allowlist or a targeted blocklist entry for extension ID inhcgfpbfdjbjogdfjbclgolkmhnooop would stop the extension from running independently of network-layer detection.
Key Points
  • 01The Chrome extension “AI Sidebar with DeepSeek AI” was removed from the Chrome Web Store in January 2026 for stealing AI conversation content, but was later relisted and continued delivering updates through Google’s CRX content delivery network.
  • 02Netskope Threat Labs found that version 1.7.3.0 no longer contained the earlier conversation-exfiltration code but added a 21-line monetization payload to blueBackground.js after a benign version 1.7.2.0 release.
  • 03The new payload opens a Bitly affiliate link to Buzzy in a foreground browser tab every time the extension updates and also sets the uninstall URL so that removing the extension generates the same referral.
  • 04The article says hundreds of users were acquiring the malicious version daily as of August 2026, with relisting on the Chrome Web Store described as the primary driver and auto-update as secondary.
  • 05Netskope recommends removing extension ID inhcgfpbfdjbjogdfjbclgolkmhnooop from managed browsers and confirming it is not present in any force-install or allowlist policy.
